If it is the only administrator account, someone with access to the server's own screen and keyboard has to reset it there.

about.title: About this interface
about.body: This is an unofficial community plugin that adds a new web interface to openmediavault. It is not made by the openmediavault project, and it changes nothing about how openmediavault works or how secure it is.

checklist.title: Set up your NAS
checklist.intro: A few things to check after installing. Each item is read from the NAS's current settings.

password.title: Change the factory password
password.body: openmediavault is installed with a password that anyone can look up. If it has not been changed yet, change it now. This page cannot check whether it has been.
password.bodyOtherAdmin: openmediavault is installed with a password for the admin account that anyone can look up. This page cannot check whether it has been changed. To change it, sign in as admin and open Your account.

https.title: Use a secure connection (HTTPS)
https.doneOnHttp: HTTPS is on, but this page was opened without it.
https.secureNoLink: Open this page with an address that starts with https://.

https.link: Open Web interface settings in the classic interface
https.readFailed: Could not read the web interface settings.

email.applyHint: After saving there, apply the changes, then send a test email.
email.link: Open Notifications in the classic interface

ssh.title: SSH
ssh.intro: SSH lets you sign in to the NAS from another computer and type commands. It is for advanced tasks; most people never need it.
ssh.pendingOnArrival: Saved SSH settings are waiting to be applied. The form shows the saved settings, which are not in effect yet.
ssh.enableHint: Each person also needs SSH access on their own account, which is set under Users.
ssh.offNote: The settings below are used when SSH is on.
ssh.portHint: The number SSH programs connect to. The usual one is 22; if you change it, tell your SSH program the new number.
ssh.portRequired: Enter a port number. The usual one is 22.
ssh.portRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 65535.
ssh.portInUse: Port {{port}} is already used by this web interface. Choose another, such as 22.
ssh.password: Allow signing in with a password
ssh.key: Allow signing in with a key
ssh.keyHint: A key is a file on your computer that proves who you are, with no password to guess. Keys are added to each account under Users.
ssh.root: Allow the root account to sign in
ssh.rootHint: root is the built-in account with full control of the NAS. It is safer to leave this off and sign in with your own account.
ssh.forwardingHint: Lets someone signed in pass other network traffic through the NAS. Leave it off unless you use it.
ssh.compressionHint: Can speed up slow connections, at the cost of some processor time.
ssh.extraHint: These lines are added as they are to the SSH server's configuration file. A mistake can stop SSH from starting, so leave this empty unless you know you need it.
ssh.warnNoMethod: With both ways of signing in turned off, nobody can sign in over SSH. To stop SSH, turn it off at the top instead.
ssh.warnTurningOff: After you apply this, new SSH connections are refused. Anything that connects over SSH, such as a backup from another computer, stops working.
ssh.warnRootPassword: The root account can sign in with only a password. Anyone who guesses it controls the NAS. Turn off root sign-in, or allow keys only.
ssh.warnKeysOnly: Only people with a key on their account can sign in now. Check that yours is added before you apply.
ssh.saved: Saved. The changes take effect when you apply them in the band at the top of the page.
ssh.saveFailed: The SSH settings were not saved.
ssh.loadFailed: Could not read the SSH settings.

disk.hardwareRaid: This is a set of disks made by a hardware RAID controller, which the NAS sees as one disk.

details.title: Health details
details.intro: Detailed readings come from the disk itself and are read only when you ask. Reading them wakes this disk if it has gone to sleep.
details.readAt: Read at {{time}}. The readings do not update by themselves.
details.noPassThrough: Some USB enclosures and virtual disks do not pass health readings through.
details.allWithin_one: The {{count}} reading is within the disk's limits.
details.allWithin_other: All {{count}} readings are within the disk's limits.

assess.pastBad: Was outside its limit in the past

5.name: Damaged areas replaced
5.meaning: Areas that went bad and were replaced by spare ones. A rising number is a warning sign.

197.name: Areas waiting to be checked
197.meaning: Areas the disk had trouble reading. It should be 0.

198.name: Areas that could not be read

199.name: Connection errors
199.meaning: Usually a loose or faulty cable, not the disk itself.

details.tableIntro: Value, Worst and Limit are the disk's own scores, usually counting down from 100 or 200. A reading is a problem when its value falls to its limit. The raw value is the disk's own count, which means something only for some readings.
details.noTable: This disk does not report a table of readings. NVMe and SAS disks report their health in another form, which is in the full report below.

result.interrupted: Interrupted, for example by a restart

details.testsEmpty: No self-test results are recorded on this disk.
details.testsEmptyHint: Some disks, such as NVMe disks, keep their results in a form shown only in the full report.
details.reportFailed: Could not read the full report.

monitoring.title: Monitoring
monitoring.watchHint: The NAS checks this disk regularly, records problems, and emails you about them when email is set up.
monitoring.globalOff: Monitoring is off for the whole NAS, so no disk is watched, even when this is ticked.
monitoring.hasTests_one: This disk has {{count}} scheduled self-test. Delete it under Scheduled self-tests below before you stop watching it.
monitoring.hasTests_other: This disk has {{count}} scheduled self-tests. Delete them under Scheduled self-tests below before you stop watching it.
monitoring.notInCheck: This disk did not report its health in the last check, so it may not support monitoring. Saving checks this.
monitoring.tempHint: Recorded at this temperature, and emailed at {{alert}}.
monitoring.tempRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 100.
monitoring.loadFailed: Could not read whether this disk is watched.
monitoring.saveFailed: The monitoring setting was not saved.

tests.title: Scheduled self-tests
tests.empty: No self-tests are scheduled for this disk. A regular short test lets the disk find problems early.
tests.notWatched: Self-tests run only while the disk is watched.

power.title: Power settings
power.intro: These settings are for hard disks. Solid-state and NVMe disks usually ignore them.
power.notSet: The NAS does not set this disk's power settings now, so the disk uses its own.
power.noRemove: Once saved, these settings can be changed but not removed. The NAS then sends all four to the disk each time it starts or wakes.
power.spindownHint: When the disk has not been used for this long, it stops spinning to save power, and starts again when it is needed, which takes a few seconds. Some disks ignore this and keep spinning; the spin-down add-on (openmediavault-spindown) can put them to sleep after the same time.

apm.label: Power-saving level
apm.0: Off: the disk does not save power by itself

power.apmHint: How hard the disk itself works to save power. From level 128 up it does not spin down by itself. Many disks do not support this setting.
power.aamHint: Lets the disk move more quietly but more slowly. Many newer disks do not support this and ignore it.
power.writeCacheHint: Makes writing faster. If the power fails suddenly, the last few seconds of writes can be lost; a battery backup (UPS) protects against that. Most disks come with it on.
power.monitorWakes: Disk monitoring checks this disk every {{interval}} and wakes it to do so, so it may never stay asleep. To let it sleep, change what happens to sleeping disks in the disk health settings.
power.applyWakes: Applying sends these settings to the disk, which wakes it if it is asleep.
power.saveFailed: The power settings were not saved.

wipe.title: Wipe this disk
wipe.intro: Wiping erases everything on the disk so it can be used for something new, such as a new file system.

blocked.system: This is the system disk: openmediavault runs from it, so it cannot be wiped.
blocked.readOnly: This disk is read-only, so it cannot be wiped.
blocked.fsInUse: It holds the file system {{name}}, which is in use.
blocked.fsInUseDo: Stop using it and unmount it under File systems first.
blocked.fsSetUp: It holds the file system {{name}}, which is set up on this NAS.
blocked.fsSetUpDo: Remove it under File systems first.
blocked.fsCreating: A file system is being created on it now.
blocked.swap: It holds swap space, disk space the NAS can use as extra memory.
blocked.raid: It is part of the RAID array <array></array>. Wiping it would damage the array.
blocked.raidDo: Remove it from the array under RAID management first.
blocked.unchecked: Could not check what this disk holds, so it cannot be wiped now.

wipe.fsLink: File systems in the classic interface
wipe.raidLink: RAID management in the classic interface
wipe.checking: Checking what is on this disk…
wipe.refusedTitle: This disk cannot be wiped now
wipe.changedBody: The disk now called {{device}} is not the one this page showed. Its details have been read again; check them before you wipe it.
wipe.goneBody: This disk is no longer connected.
wipe.consequence: Everything on this disk is erased: its partitions, file systems and files. This cannot be undone.

holds.fsUnused: The file system {{name}} ({{type}}, {{size}}). It is not used on this NAS. Its files are lost.
holds.none: No file system was found. Anything else on it, such as data from another computer, is erased too.
holds.untraceable: This NAS also has storage that this page cannot trace to a disk, such as encrypted disks, LVM or ZFS. If this disk is part of it, wiping it destroys that storage and its files.
holds.settingsKept: Its monitoring and power settings are kept.
holds.fsUnusedNoSize: The file system {{name}} ({{type}}). It is not used on this NAS. Its files are lost.

wipe.quickHint: Erases the partition table and the start and end of the disk, so the NAS sees it as empty. Takes a few seconds. The old files stay on the disk until they are overwritten, and recovery tools could still find them.
wipe.secureHint: Overwrites the whole disk once, so the old files cannot be recovered. Takes many hours: often 2 hours or more for each TB on a hard disk. You can stop it, but the disk is then only partly wiped. On a solid-state disk it may not reach every part of the disk.
wipe.secureReload: A secure wipe keeps running on the NAS if you reload this page or sign out, but this page can then no longer show it or stop it.
wipe.typeHint: The Wipe disk button is available once the name matches.
wipe.quickRunning: Quick wipe. This takes a few seconds.
wipe.secureRunning: Secure wipe. This takes many hours. You can leave this page or sign out; the wipe continues on the NAS. Its progress is shown here and in Tasks while you stay signed in.
wipe.stopBody: The part already overwritten stays erased; the rest of the disk is not wiped. Run a quick wipe afterwards so the NAS sees the disk as empty.
wipe.doneBody: It is now empty and ready to use. To store files on it, create a file system on it.
wipe.createFsLink: Create a file system in the classic interface
wipe.failedTitle: The wipe of {{device}} did not finish.
wipe.failedBody: Part of the disk may already be erased. Read the output for the reason.
wipe.stoppedBody: The part already overwritten is erased; the rest is not. Run a quick wipe so the NAS sees the disk as empty.

smart.title: Disk health
smart.intro: Whether the NAS watches your disks for signs of failure, and how it tells you.

overview.off: Monitoring is off. The NAS does not check your disks and will not tell you when one starts to fail.
overview.some: Monitoring is on for {{watched}} of {{total}} disks.
overview.all: Monitoring is on for every disk.
overview.emailOff: Email is not set up, so problems are only recorded in the NAS's log.
overview.emailLink: Email settings in the classic interface
overview.eventsNote: Alerts are sent only while "S.M.A.R.T." is ticked under Notification > Events in the classic interface (it is from the factory).
overview.eventsLink: Notification events in the classic interface
overview.emailFailed: Could not read the email settings.
overview.watchFailed_one: Could not read whether {{count}} disk is watched.
overview.watchFailed_other: Could not read whether {{count}} disks are watched.
overview.settingsFailed: Could not read the monitoring settings.
overview.classicLink: Disk health in the classic interface

settings.watchHint: The NAS checks each watched disk regularly, records problems in its log, and emails you when email is set up. Choose the disks to watch on the Overview or on each disk's page.
settings.watchOffWarn: With this off, no disk is checked and no self-test runs.
settings.intervalHint: How often the NAS checks each watched disk. Every 30 minutes suits most homes.
settings.intervalOdd: Now every {{seconds}} seconds, set elsewhere. Saving rounds it to whole minutes.
settings.intervalRange: Enter a whole number of minutes from 1 to 1440.
settings.asleep: When a disk is asleep at check time
settings.asleepHint: A disk that is asleep at every check is not checked until it is awake at one.
settings.asleepTestsRun: Scheduled self-tests still run, and wake the disk.
settings.asleepTestsSkipped: A self-test due while the disk is asleep is skipped too.

mode.never: Check it anyway; the check wakes the disk up
mode.sleep: Skip only disks in deep sleep; a disk that has only spun down is woken up
mode.standby: Skip the check, so the disk stays asleep (recommended)
mode.idle: Skip also while the disk is spinning but resting; checks happen only while it is busy

modeShort.never: Sleeping disks are woken for each check.
modeShort.sleep: Only disks in deep sleep are left asleep.
modeShort.idle: Resting and sleeping disks are left alone.

settings.tempWarn: Warn when a disk gets too hot
settings.tempHint: The NAS records it at this temperature and emails you at {{alert}}. Solid-state and NVMe disks often run hotter than hard disks; set their own limit on each disk's page.
settings.tempRange: Enter a whole number from 1 to 100.
settings.tempDiffHint: Writes a line in the NAS's log each time a disk's temperature changes by this much.
settings.loadFailed: Could not read the monitoring settings.
settings.saveFailed: The monitoring settings were not saved.

tests.intro: A self-test is a check the disk runs on itself. A short test takes a few minutes; a long test reads the whole disk and takes hours. The disk keeps working meanwhile, a little slower. The NAS starts each test at its time; its result is in the disk's health details.
tests.globalOff: Monitoring is off for the whole NAS, so no self-test runs.

runs.notWatched: No, the disk is not watched
runs.notConnected: No, the disk is not connected

tests.runNowNotWatched: Watch this disk first; the NAS starts tests only on watched disks.
tests.classicLink: Scheduled tests in the classic interface

typeHint.S: A quick check of the disk's main parts. Takes a few minutes.
typeHint.L: Reads the whole disk. Takes hours on a large disk, and the disk is slower meanwhile.
typeHint.C: Looks for damage from shipping. Only some disks support it. Takes a few minutes.
typeHint.O: Updates the disk's own health readings. Takes a few minutes.

when.monthly: On day {{day}} of every month at {{hour}}

dialog.diskNotWatchedHint: A self-test runs only on a watched disk. Turn on watching on the disk's page.
dialog.dayOver28: Months without this day are skipped.
dialog.customHint: The test runs when all four match. With both a day of the month and a weekday, it runs only on days that are both.
dialog.enable: Run this test on its schedule
dialog.enableHint: Untick to keep the test but stop it running.
dialog.oddValue: Choose one of the values offered; {{value}} was set elsewhere.
dialog.longHourly: A long test takes hours. Choose an hour, or it would start again before it finishes.
dialog.longDaily: A long test every day keeps the disk busy for hours each day.

tests.deleteBody: It no longer runs once you apply the changes. The disk's past results are kept.
tests.runBodyShort: The disk checks itself for a few minutes. It wakes up if it is asleep. Your files are not changed, and the disk can be used meanwhile.
tests.runBodyLong: The disk reads its whole surface. This takes hours on a large disk, and the disk is slower meanwhile. It wakes up if it is asleep. Your files are not changed.
tests.runFailed: The test could not be started on {{device}}.
tests.runStarted: {{device}} started a {{test}}. The disk runs it by itself; the result appears in its health details when it finishes, in about {{duration}}.
tests.runUnclear: The NAS sent the test to {{device}}, but the disk's reply does not say it started. Read the output for the reason.
tests.loadFailed: Could not read the scheduled self-tests.
tests.empty: No self-tests are scheduled. A regular short test lets each disk find problems early.

setup.title: Set up disk monitoring
setup.preflightTitle: Some changes are not applied yet
setup.preflightBody: Apply or undo them before you set up monitoring, so that only these changes are applied at the end.
setup.needCheck: To list the disks that can report their health, the NAS reads every disk. This wakes any disk that has gone to sleep.
setup.usingCheck: Using the disk health checked at {{time}}.
setup.badStatus: Its health could not be read, so watching it may not work.
setup.notListed: Not listed because they report no health readings: {{list}}.
setup.allWatched: Every disk that can report its health is already watched.

tests.label: Regular self-test
tests.both: Both: a short test every week and a long test every month
tests.longHint: A long test reads the whole disk and takes hours; the disk is slower meanwhile.
tests.keeps_one: {{device}} already has {{count}} scheduled self-test and keeps it.
tests.keeps_other: {{device}} already has {{count}} scheduled self-tests and keeps them.

setup.sleepHint: The NAS skips a check while a disk is asleep, instead of waking it.
setup.temp: Warn me when a disk gets too hot
setup.emailLater: You can run this now and set up email afterwards; alerts start reaching you once both are applied.
setup.summaryTitle: Ready to set up disk monitoring

sum.globalOn: Turn on disk monitoring for the NAS.
sum.short_one: Run a short self-test on {{count}} disk {{when}}.
sum.short_other: Run a short self-test on {{count}} disks {{when}}.
sum.long_one: Run a long self-test on {{count}} disk {{when}}.
sum.long_other: Run a long self-test on {{count}} disks {{when}}.
sum.whenMonthly: on day {{day}} of every month at {{hour}}
sum.keeps: {{list}} already have scheduled self-tests and keep them.
sum.sleepOn: Skip checks while a disk is asleep, so it stays asleep.
sum.sleepOff: Check disks even when they are asleep, which wakes them.
sum.tempOn: Record a disk that reaches {{limit}}, and email you when it reaches {{alert}}.
sum.emailOff: Email is not set up, so problems are only recorded in the NAS's log for now.
sum.interval: The NAS checks each watched disk every {{interval}}. You can change this in the settings.
sum.apply: Then the changes are applied, which restarts disk monitoring. Nothing on your disks is changed.

step.global: Turn on monitoring for the NAS
